Plastics Past and Present: Understanding historical trends of microplastic consumption in California marine food webs to better inform future marine management

R/HCE-40B

PROJECT HIGHLIGHT

This project uses fish specimens from museum collections to trace the history of microplastic pollution in Southern California waters from the 1940s to today. Early findings reveal that microplastics have been present in California marine fish since at least 1949, with widespread contamination across all feeding types by the 1970s. This study establishes the first long-term baseline for microplastic pollution in Pacific coastal waters, providing critical information to guide future management decisions.

 

PROJECT SUMMARY

Tiny plastic particles smaller than 5 millimeters, called microplastics and nanoplastics, are now found throughout the world's oceans. But we know little about which marine species are most affected or how long this problem has existed. This project examines microplastic consumption in six ecologically distinct fish species along the Southern California coast, using preserved specimens from the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Scripps Institution of Oceanography and Occidental College. The species studied represent different feeding styles, from plant-eaters to fish-eaters, and live at different ocean depths, from shallow coastal waters to the deep sea.

The research team has completed the dissection and processing of 353 individual fish and is using Raman spectroscopy to identify microplastic particles approaching nanoscale sizes. Preliminary findings show that microplastics appear in all species examined, regardless of what they eat or where they live. The earliest detection was in a fish from 1949, and by the 1970s every species studied contained individuals with microplastics. Interestingly, not every fish sampled contains microplastics, even in recent years, suggesting some individuals may clear contaminants from their digestive systems or avoid consuming them.

The study has identified a wide variety of plastic types, with polyethylene being the most common, followed by other plastics such as polyurethane, PEVA and plastic fibers like nylon and polyester. Most plastic types appear across all species, indicating fish are consuming microplastics generally rather than targeting specific types.
